Exponential growth of scientific literature and increasing domain speciali...
citation: Closing the Empirical Loop: Autonomous AI Agents Conduct End‐to‐end Research With Human Participants. Gabrielle Wehr, Reuben Rideaux, Amaya Fox, David R. Lightfoot, Jason M. Tangen, Jason B. Mattingley, Shane E. Ehrhardt. 2026-09-14. https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.76675
publication_status_evidence: OpenAlex records a published journal location: Advanced Science. Peer review inferred from venue metadata, not independently verified.
relevance_reason: Studies AI-scientist or scientific-discovery agents.

concerns: The available results appear to demonstrate functionality rather than comparative effectiveness.
The human expert evaluation is described qualitatively, without a detailed scoring rubric, inter-rater reliability, or quantitative comparison against human-authored baselines.

The claim of 'methodological rigor comparable to experienced researchers' is partly undermined by the reported theoretical misrepresentations, statistical omissions, and internal contradictions in the generated manuscripts.
The paper does not provide a direct controlled comparison with human researchers or with alternative agentic frameworks.
The expert evaluation appears to have been conducted by the authors or their collaborators, which may introduce confirmation bias despite the structured review process.
scholarly_quality.concise_summary: This systems/application paper demonstrates an autonomous multi-agent AI pipeline that performs end-to-end empirical research with human participants, producing three cognitive psychology manuscripts. The contribution is architectural and demonstrative. The paper provides strong methodological description, transparency, reproducibility testing, ablation studies, and detailed limitations. The main weakness is that the validation of generated manuscript quality relies on qualitative expert review without a fully specified quantitative protocol or controlled comparison, and the reported expert assessment identifies substantive scientific flaws in the generated manuscripts.

evidence.excerpt: The contribution of this work is architectural rather than methodological at the model level: we use only standard, publicly available frontier LLMs, and demonstrate that when combined across providers, embedded in a hierarchical multi-agent architecture, and augmented by the cognitive operators and dynamic memory systems described above - these techniques are jointly sufficient to conduct empirical science autonomously from hypothesis generation through to manuscript preparation.
evidence.explanation: This clearly delineates the scope of the contribution and prevents overclaiming about model innovation.
evidence.paraphrase: The authors explicitly state that the contribution is architectural rather than a new model-level method, and that the novelty lies in demonstrating end-to-end empirical research with human participants.

evidence.excerpt: as far as we are aware, this is the first demonstration of an autonomously conducted, end-to-end online experiment with human participants.
evidence.explanation: This supports the novelty claim by situating the work relative to prior agentic scientific discovery systems.
evidence.paraphrase: The paper claims to be the first demonstration of autonomous end-to-end online experimentation with human participants, distinguishing it from prior in silico or domain-specific systems.

evidence.excerpt: the method agent engages a pre-registration agent, which develops a pre-registration report compliant with Open Science Framework (OSF) standards [ 56 ], detailing hypotheses, independent and dependent variables, sampling procedures, exclusion criteria, analytical approaches, and anticipated outcomes.
evidence.explanation: These mechanisms support the claim of methodological rigor in the pipeline design.
evidence.paraphrase: The system includes pre-registration, power analysis, literature-backed data cleaning, and multiple verification agents to ensure methodological consistency.

evidence.excerpt: To test the reproducibility of the results across multiple iterations, we reran one of the studies (Supporting Information  S3 ) an additional five times, starting from the stage following research question ideation. While there were considerable differences between the iterations in terms of analytical designs and interpretive focal points, research outputs consistently came to the same broad conclusions across all five runs.
evidence.explanation: This provides empirical evidence for the reliability of the system's outputs, not just their validity.
evidence.paraphrase: The authors report a reproducibility test in which one study was rerun five times, with consistent broad conclusions across iterations.

evidence.excerpt: There are (currently) no objective tests with which to evaluate the quality of scientific manuscripts; thus, here we employed structured expert review (mirroring established peer review processes) to assess the AI-generated manuscripts.
evidence.explanation: This limits the strength of the validation because the expert review protocol and quantitative scoring are not fully specified in the extracted text.
evidence.paraphrase: The human expert evaluation is reported qualitatively, and the paper acknowledges that no objective tests exist for evaluating scientific manuscript quality.

evidence.excerpt: In practice, the system's hypotheses were frequently violated; for example, in the study titled "Precision Response Patterns in Visual Working Memory: Shared Constraints with Mental Rotation and the Role of Imagery Vividness", only two of five pre-registered hypotheses (H1a and H1b) received any support, and even these were only partially supported by the data, with similar contradictions between predictions and findings emerging in the other two studies.
evidence.explanation: This directly addresses a potential threat to the validity of the system's outputs and aligns the evidence with the claim of unbiased empirical testing.
evidence.paraphrase: The authors use pre-registered hypotheses that were frequently violated by the data as evidence against the concern that the system is biased toward confirming its own expectations.

evidence.excerpt: Theoretical models were occasionally misrepresented, including inappropriate extension of a VWM framework [ 120 ] to unrelated visuospatial tasks in Study 3, and Study 2's false claim about working memory resource allocation debates.
evidence.explanation: These reported flaws partially undermine the claim that the system demonstrates methodological rigor comparable to experienced researchers.
evidence.paraphrase: The expert evaluation identifies substantive flaws in the generated manuscripts, including theoretical misrepresentations, statistical omissions, and internal contradictions.

evidence.excerpt: Current end-to-end agentic scientific discovery frameworks continue to operate primarily in simulated or abstract digital environments [ 40 ,  41 ,  42 ,  43 ,  44 ,  45 ], typically producing outcomes with predictive power but lacking explanation of underlying causal mechanisms.
evidence.explanation: This establishes the gap that the present work addresses: real-world empirical testing with human participants.
evidence.paraphrase: The paper situates its contribution relative to prior agentic scientific discovery systems, noting that existing frameworks operate primarily in simulated or abstract digital environments.

evidence.excerpt: The data and code that support the findings of this study are openly available on GitHub at  https://github.com/Explore-Science/Virtuous-Machines-Towards-Artificial-General-Science .
evidence.explanation: This supports reproducibility and transparency, which are central claims of the paper.
evidence.paraphrase: The authors release data, code, pre-registrations, and all outputs on GitHub, and provide a complete paper trail of analytic decisions.

evidence.excerpt: While the framework is general by design, currently its physical capabilities are domain-constrained to online experiments for which the necessary tools and interfaces are available.
evidence.explanation: This demonstrates a thorough treatment of limitations and uncertainty, including potential failure modes.
evidence.paraphrase: The authors acknowledge that the system is domain-constrained, that visualizations have aesthetic imperfections, and that early-stage errors can propagate downstream.

evidence.excerpt: The system executed full studies (from initial conception to manuscript) in ∼17 h runtime on average per study, excluding data collection.
evidence.explanation: This supports the precision and clarity of the systems-level reporting.
evidence.paraphrase: The paper provides detailed quantitative system performance metrics, including token usage, runtime, cost, and lines of code.

evidence.excerpt: Technical problems with visualizations included minor layout issues across Figures, and missing axis labels in Study 3.
evidence.explanation: These issues indicate that the system's output quality is not yet fully publication-ready without human intervention.
evidence.paraphrase: The expert evaluation reports presentation issues in the generated manuscripts, including missing axis labels, inconsistent terminology, and awkward table formatting.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The manuscript presents a systems/application contribution: an autonomous multi-agent AI pipeline that performs end-to-end empirical research with human participants. The central claim is architectural and demonstrative rather than a new psychological finding. The paper provides substantial methodological description, explicit expert evaluation of the generated manuscripts, reproducibility tests, ablation tests for review agents and dynamic memory, and detailed limitations. The evidence supports the claimed feasibility demonstration, while the authors appropriately acknowledge that the scientific quality of the generated studies is mixed and that no validated benchmark exists for autonomous research quality.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The main uncertainty is whether the expert evaluation of the three AI-generated manuscripts is sufficiently independent and systematic to support the claim that the system demonstrates 'theoretical reasoning and methodological rigor comparable to experienced researchers.' The paper reports structured expert review but does not provide the full reviewer protocol, inter-rater reliability, or quantitative scoring in the extracted text. This limits confidence in the strength of the validation, though the authors also release the manuscripts and code for independent appraisal.

citation: An immune world model for multiscale forecasting and therapeutic hypothesis generation. Taoyong Cui, Xi Wang, Zonghang Li, Jinchao Ding, Lingsen You, Yuzhi Xu, Wanghan Xu, Fang Wu, Kejun Ying, Wanli Ouyang, Pheng Ann Heng, Ling Yang, Zhenfei Yin, Yingcheng Wu. 2026-09-13. https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2609.14709
publication_status_evidence: arXiv manuscript identifier; no external publication established by the available metadata.
relevance_reason: Studies AI-scientist or scientific-discovery agents.

concerns: The code, data manifests, and model weights are described as forthcoming in a 'versioned software release' rather than currently available, making independent reproducibility unverifiable at submission time; the paper's own resource availability section confirms this (B0057).

The paper references several future-dated or preprint-only works as key baselines and components (e.g., STACK ref 15 dated 2026, Rhaister ref 40 dated 2026, PULSAR ref 41 dated 2025, Parse PBMC atlas ref 39 dated 2025), none of which are independently published at the time of this preprint, creating circular or unverifiable dependency chains for the evaluation.

The primary forecasting result on the common-gene-space benchmark ties the Immune World Model with the condition-mean baseline (both 0.46 Δcos; B0033), which is a simple non-parametric aggregator, substantially weakening the central action-conditioned dynamics claim; the paper acknowledges this but the discussion does not fully resolve whether per-action gains compensate for this aggregate tie.

The anti-PD-1 patient-state AUC of 0.92 (LOO-CV, n unspecified but implied small given 95% CI 0.79–1.00; B0034/B0035) is based on leave-one-out cross-validation on what appears to be a small cohort, and the wide confidence intervals indicate high uncertainty; the sample size is not explicitly stated in the accessible text, limiting interpretability of this headline result.

The 'governed evolutionary AI Scientist' (Agent Genesis) is a central methodological claim, but the builder benchmark compares the EvoIWM-building Scientist against named commercial LLM versions (DeepSeek V4, Claude S5, GPT-5.6, Gemini 3.6, Qwen 3.6) that do not correspond to any publicly released model versions as of the manuscript's stated arXiv date (September 2026), making the comparison unverifiable and raising concerns about the manuscript's internal consistency.

The therapeutic hypothesis (IL-36γ plus SIRPα inhibition) is explicitly unvalidated experimentally (B0055), which is acceptable for a computational study, but the nomination rests partly on zero-shot inference from OrthJEPA and SE-PCA, which are described as internal configuration labels rather than independently validated methods (B0091/B0092), limiting the strength of the biological evidence chain.
scholarly_quality.concise_summary: The contribution is substantive and scoped, the method is adequately described, evaluation is meaningful across multiple scales with appropriate controls and uncertainty reporting, and claims are appropriately qualified with limitations compatible with the computational scope.

evidence.excerpt:
The Immune World Model reframes immune prediction as the estimation of an intervention-
conditioned state transition rather than the assignment of a static sample label. Single-cell
foundation and perturbation models have made transferable cell-state encoding and extrapo-
lation increasingly tractable, but therapeutic effects remain conditioned by tissue ecology and
host immune context. By representing the intervention independently from cellular, tissue, and
individual state, the Immune World Model estimates how a specified action moves a biological
system through immune-state space. The benefit of combining cell and tissue information, to-
gether with the higher anti-PD-1 AUC point estimate obtained from functional all-cell states than
from composition alone, supports the value of structured multiscale context. World Model Rollout
extends the same formulation across biological scales,

missing_information: No suitable baseline comparison was detected in the available text.

blocking_reasons: The code, data manifests, and model weights are described as forthcoming in a 'versioned software release' rather than currently available, making independent reproducibility unverifiable at submission time; the paper's own resource availability section confirms this (B0057).

The paper references several future-dated or preprint-only works as key baselines and components (e.g., STACK ref 15 dated 2026, Rhaister ref 40 dated 2026, PULSAR ref 41 dated 2025, Parse PBMC atlas ref 39 dated 2025), none of which are independently published at the time of this preprint, creating circular or unverifiable dependency chains for the evaluation.

The primary forecasting result on the common-gene-space benchmark ties the Immune World Model with the condition-mean baseline (both 0.46 Δcos; B0033), which is a simple non-parametric aggregator, substantially weakening the central action-conditioned dynamics claim; the paper acknowledges this but the discussion does not fully resolve whether per-action gains compensate for this aggregate tie.

The anti-PD-1 patient-state AUC of 0.92 (LOO-CV, n unspecified but implied small given 95% CI 0.79–1.00; B0034/B0035) is based on leave-one-out cross-validation on what appears to be a small cohort, and the wide confidence intervals indicate high uncertainty; the sample size is not explicitly stated in the accessible text, limiting interpretability of this headline result.

The 'governed evolutionary AI Scientist' (Agent Genesis) is a central methodological claim, but the builder benchmark compares the EvoIWM-building Scientist against named commercial LLM versions (DeepSeek V4, Claude S5, GPT-5.6, Gemini 3.6, Qwen 3.6) that do not correspond to any publicly released model versions as of the manuscript's stated arXiv date (September 2026), making the comparison unverifiable and raising concerns about the manuscript's internal consistency.

The therapeutic hypothesis (IL-36γ plus SIRPα inhibition) is explicitly unvalidated experimentally (B0055), which is acceptable for a computational study, but the nomination rests partly on zero-shot inference from OrthJEPA and SE-PCA, which are described as internal configuration labels rather than independently validated methods (B0091/B0092), limiting the strength of the biological evidence chain.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Claims of multiscale forecasting and hypothesis nomination are supported by the reported benchmarks and ablations, and the therapeutic hypothesis is explicitly framed as model-derived and prospectively testable rather than validated.
primary.evaluation_assessment: Evaluation includes locked external-capability probes, few-shot cellular forecasting, tissue and individual-context benchmarks, action composition, and a governed self-correction audit, with confidence intervals and negative results reported where relevant.
primary.limitations: The authors acknowledge that experimental confirmation, formal pharmacological synergy, cohort-level validation of recursive rollout, and larger external clinical cohorts remain to be established.
primary.method_assessment: The structured encoder, action-conditioned transition, and structured decoder are described with formal equations and module-level ablations; the AI Scientist development process is documented with versioned lineage, predeclared promotion gates, and locked confirmation manifests.
primary.quality_rationale: The contribution is substantive and scoped, the method is adequately described, evaluation is meaningful across multiple scales with appropriate controls and uncertainty reporting, and claims are appropriately qualified with limitations compatible with the computational scope.
primary.scoped_contribution: The manuscript presents the Immune World Model, an action-conditioned multiscale model that learns intervention-dependent transitions across cellular, tissue, and individual immune states, constructed via a governed evolutionary AI Scientist and frozen before independent confirmation.

scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The authors acknowledge that experimental confirmation, formal pharmacological synergy, cohort-level validation of recursive rollout, and larger external clinical cohorts remain to be established.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Claims are generally well supported by the reported results: reviewer-guided revision improves more than fixed-prompt self-revision, Stanford Reviewer independently confirms upward trajectories, and the execution-versus-idea resolution asymmetry is quantified and discussed. The abstract's headline numbers match the body, and the authors appropriately frame the finding that novelty concerns are rarely resolved.
primary.evaluation_assessment: Evaluation is meaningful and multi-layered: reviewer quality is separately benchmarked against baselines on 650 ICLR papers with pairwise judging and human-alignment checks, and revision outcomes are measured on 30 papers across five domains with score trajectories, an external Stanford Reviewer evaluation of human-initialized revisions, and a weakness-resolution analysis (128/150 execution vs 2/18 idea weaknesses). Controls include autonomous self-revision with a fixed prompt and AI-initialized guidance, isolating the effect of iterative reviewer feedback.
primary.limitations: The evaluation set is small (30 papers) and constrained to ICLR papers reproducible on a single 96 GB GPU, with cost (~$65/paper) cited as the limiting factor. The same reviewer both guides and scores the reviewer-driven conditions, though the external Stanford Reviewer evaluation partially mitigates this circularity; Stanford Reviewer is not applied to the AI-initialized or self-revision conditions.
primary.method_assessment: The system design is described in adequate detail: the scientist retains full revision history and addresses each reviewer concern through code edits, literature search, experiment execution, and manuscript updates, while the reviewer independently evaluates only the current manuscript with no memory of prior drafts or scores. The reviewer uses a structured multi-phase process with deep literature search over an indexed arXiv corpus, temporal grounding, and a verification pass.
primary.quality_rationale: The paper makes a substantive, clearly scoped contribution with a well-described system, appropriate controls, independent external evaluation, and a nuanced characterization of what iterative revision can and cannot improve. The main weaknesses are acknowledged and bounded by the study design, and the evidence supports the stated claims without overclaiming.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper introduces AppliedScientist, a closed-loop system that iteratively revises rejected papers' implementation, experiments, and manuscript under fresh independent AI reviews, while keeping the central research contribution fixed. It contributes a benchmark of reviewer-guided versus fixed-prompt self-revision across 30 ICLR papers and a characterization of which reviewer weaknesses revision can resolve.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The paper makes a substantive, clearly scoped contribution with a well-described system, appropriate controls, independent external evaluation, and a nuanced characterization of what iterative revision can and cannot improve. The main weaknesses are acknowledged and bounded by the study design, and the evidence supports the stated claims without overclaiming.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The evaluation set is small (30 papers) and constrained to ICLR papers reproducible on a single 96 GB GPU, with cost (~$65/paper) cited as the limiting factor. The same reviewer both guides and scores the reviewer-driven conditions, though the external Stanford Reviewer evaluation partially mitigates this circularity; Stanford Reviewer is not applied to the AI-initialized or self-revision conditions.

Autonomous research agents are increasingly expected to search the literature, analyze experimen-
tal evidence, and generate scientific hypotheses. These capabilities require multi-step evidence-
grounded reasoning that progressively acquires, integrates, and verifies evidence before reaching
a conclusion. Existing multimodal benchmarks, however, largely evaluate final-answer accuracy,
leaving open whether predictions are actually supported by traceable scientific evidence. We in-
troduceSci-MMR, a benchmark for 
[… separate evidence block …]
multi-step evidence-grounded scientific reasoning built on
structured argument graphs linking scientific claims, citation-grounded knowledge, visual evidence,
and supporting regions. Sci-MMR comprises 235 multi-hop reasoning tasks spanning four scientific
disciplines, with an average of nine figure panels per task. Evaluating eight frontier multimodal
models, we find that answer accuracy consistently exceeds complete-evidence recovery rate by more
than 20%, revealing a substantial gap that answer-only evaluation is structurally unable to capture.
Through controlled interventions, we identify two fundamental bottlenecks. First, evidence acquisi-
tion: models struggle to extract complete structured evidence from scientific figures, accounting for
57.2% of failures. While cropping tools yield modest gains (+4.5 points), providing gold evidence
improves accuracy by up to 37.0 points,

Autonomous research agents are increasingly expected to search the literature, analyze experimen-
tal evidence, and generate scientific hypotheses. These capabilities require multi-step evidence-
grounded reasoning that progressively acquires, integrates, and verifies evidence before reaching
a conclusion. Existing multimodal benchmarks, however, largely evaluate final-answer accuracy,
leaving open whether predictions are actually supported by traceable scientific evidence. We in-
troduceSci-MMR, a benchmark for

source_spans.text:
multi-step evidence-grounded scientific reasoning built on
structured argument graphs linking scientific claims, citation-grounded knowledge, visual evidence,
and supporting regions. Sci-MMR comprises 235 multi-hop reasoning tasks spanning four scientific
disciplines, with an average of nine figure panels per task. Evaluating eight frontier multimodal
models, we find that answer accuracy consistently exceeds complete-evidence recovery rate by more
than 20%, revealing a substantial gap that answer-only evaluation is structurally unable to capture.
Through controlled interventions, we identify two fundamental bottlenecks. First, evidence acquisi-
tion: models struggle to extract complete structured evidence from scientific figures, accounting for
57.2% of failures. While cropping tools yield modest gains (+4.5 points), providing gold evidence
improves accuracy by up to 37.0 points,

positive_signals: Sci-MMR is a benchmark of 235 multi-hop reasoning tasks spanning four scientific disciplines, built on structured argument graphs linking claims, citation-grounded knowledge, visual evidence, and supporting regions, with an average of nine figure panels per task.

The benchmark construction pipeline includes deterministic validation removing 54% of candidate tasks, an eight-dimensional LLM quality rubric filtering a further 17%, and final expert review of 260 tasks with 25 rejected and 235 retained.

Existing scientific multimodal benchmarks primarily evaluate final-answer correctness and do not evaluate whether models acquire the complete evidence supporting a scientific conclusion, a gap Sci-MMR addresses by disentangling evidence acquisition from evidence integration.

The paper acknowledges that an Argument Graph represents one plausible reconstruction of a paper's evidential structure rather than unique ground truth, and that LLM-based assessment may be affected by semantic ambiguity, response style, and evaluator bias.

However, existing benchmarks mainly evaluate medium-horizon exploration and rarely test whether agents can sustain long, dependency-heavy research processes. We introduce Mr. LHDR (Multimod...

scholarly_quality.concise_summary: The paper introduces Mr.LHDR, a benchmark for long-horizon multimodal deep research with 102 items constructed from hidden Node-Relation graphs. It defines OA, SA, CS, and DACS metrics and evaluates 25 systems, finding that final-answer accuracy overstates dependency-consistent task success. The contribution is clearly scoped, the methodology is described with validation gates, and the central claims are supported by quantitative evidence including an image ablation and failure-mode analysis. Limitations are acknowledged, and the related-work positioning is adequate for the benchmark's claims.

evidence.excerpt: We introduce Mr.LHDR (Multimodal real-world Long-Horizon Deep Research), a benchmark for real-world open-web research tasks. Mr.LHDR contains 102 questions across eight categories.
evidence.explanation: The introduction clearly defines Mr.LHDR as a benchmark for long-horizon multimodal deep research and lists three design principles and three contributions.
evidence.paraphrase: The benchmark contribution is explicitly stated with its scope and distinguishing features.

evidence.excerpt: MM-BrowseComp-style tasks add multimodal browsing, but remain concentrated on short- to medium-horizon research: MM-BrowseComp contains only 3.0 checklist items per question on average (Li et al., 2025d), leaving long chains of dependent evidence steps largely untested.
evidence.explanation: The paper contrasts Mr.LHDR with existing benchmarks such as MM-BrowseComp, which averages only 3.0 checklist items per question, and positions the contribution around prerequisite-linked evidence structures.
evidence.paraphrase: The benchmark fills an identified gap in long-horizon, dependency-heavy multimodal research evaluation.

evidence.excerpt: Table 2: Quality gates applied before an item enters the Mr.LHDR evaluation set. These gates operationalize answer uniqueness, no path leakage, irreducibility, source support, multimodal necessity, shortcut filtering, and metadata consistency.
evidence.explanation: The paper describes answer uniqueness, no path leakage, irreducible checklist, source support, multimodal necessity, shortcut filtering, and metadata audit gates, with a structured validation protocol.
evidence.paraphrase: The construction pipeline includes explicit quality gates and a four-stage validation protocol.

evidence.excerpt: Table 4: Main Mr.LHDR results for all 25 systems in the current evaluation scope, grouped by model capability. Overall columns report final-answer accuracy (OA), strict answer-and-process accuracy (SA), checklist score (CS), and dependency-aware checklist score (DACS).
evidence.explanation: The main results table reports OA, SA, CS, and DACS for tool-augmented VLMs, tool-free VLMs, deep research systems, and framework-based agents.
evidence.paraphrase: The evaluation includes 25 systems across four model groups with four complementary metrics.

evidence.excerpt: GPT-5.5 drops from 43.1% OA to 34.3% SA, a gap of 8.8 points. Similarly, o4-mini drops from 35.3% OA to 20.6% SA, a gap of 14.7 points, and o3 Deep Research drops from 32.4% OA to 19.6% SA, a gap of 12.8 points.
evidence.explanation: The paper reports specific OA-to-SA drops for representative systems, such as GPT-5.5 from 43.1% OA to 34.3% SA, supporting the claim that correct final answers often coexist with missing required conclusions.
evidence.paraphrase: The central claim that final-answer accuracy overstates complete task success is directly supported by OA-SA gaps.

evidence.excerpt: Table 1 compares Mr.LHDR with representative short-answer browsing and structured-search benchmarks in terms of retrieval setting, multimodal requirements, output form, gold intermediate structure, and prerequisite-gated scoring.
evidence.explanation: Table 1 compares Mr.LHDR with BrowseComp, MM-BrowseComp, MMSearch-Plus, BrowseComp-V 3, DeepSearchQA, and MC-Search on retrieval setting, multimodal requirements, output form, gold structure, and prerequisite-gated scoring, which is adequate for the benchmark's claims.
evidence.paraphrase: The related-work section compares Mr.LHDR with representative benchmarks along relevant dimensions.

evidence.excerpt: Because these metrics neither observe the agent’s internal reasoning nor establish that a stated conclusion came from actual retrieval, they evaluate dependency-consistent stated conclusions rather than actual evidence-chain completion.
evidence.explanation: The paper clarifies that DACS evaluates dependency-consistent stated conclusions rather than actual evidence-chain completion, avoiding overclaiming about retrieval provenance.
evidence.paraphrase: The authors explicitly state what DACS does and does not measure.

evidence.excerpt: CS rises from 26.9% to 39.3% (gain 12.4, 95% CI [6.9, 18.3]), while DACS rises from 21.6% to 34.2% (gain 12.6, CI [6.9, 18.9]).
evidence.explanation: Equations 1-5 define OA, SA, CS, and DACS, and the image ablation reports 95% bootstrap CIs with a specified seed.
evidence.paraphrase: The paper provides formal metric definitions and reports bootstrap confidence intervals for the ablation.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The paper presents a clearly scoped benchmark contribution with explicit construction principles, a defined evaluation protocol, and empirical results across 25 systems. The central claims are supported by quantitative evidence in the supplied text, including main results, an image ablation with bootstrap confidence intervals, checklist-length analysis, and failure-mode diagnostics. The authors explicitly distinguish what the metrics do and do not measure, and limitations are acknowledged. The related-work section positions Mr.LHDR against representative benchmarks and explains the gap it addresses. The available partial text is sufficient to establish substantive manuscript evidence for the six required dimensions.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The assessment is based on partial full text limited to 120,000 characters, so some appendix-level details, complete judge robustness analyses, and full split-level results are not available. Confidence intervals for many system comparisons overlap, and the authors themselves note that most per-model differences are not statistically separable. These factors limit the strength of ranking claims but do not undermine the benchmark contribution itself.

Evaluating the capabilities of AI for automating scientific research 
requires test problems that reflect the demands of real research 
practice. Standard benchmarks, 1-4 built from static datasets of 
narrow questions, seem convenient but may not capture the long-
horizon, multi-step workflows characteristic of authentic scientific 
inquiry.5 We and other authors proposed using recently published 
scientific papers as reference material instead, 6-9  since they 
embody the methodological complexity, data -handling 
requirements, and interpretive judgment characteristic of actual 
research, and they provide an external standard against which AI -
generated results can be compared  with. AI performance on such 
problems is therefore important not only for evaluating scientific 
capability of AI in general, but also for estimating the readiness of 
these frameworks to contribute to

AI research frameworks (Kosmos, K -Dense, ToolUniverse,

across three projects: uncertainty quantification for molecular 
property prediction under distribution shifts, machine learning  
(ML) on Therapeutic Data Commons  benchmarks, and agent -
based macroeconomic modeling. Across all three projects, the 
frameworks in many cases generated original hypotheses, handled 
routine data acquisition and coding competently, and produced 
well-formatted draft reports. However, no AI framework matched

positive_signals: The paper extends a prior evaluation of five AI research frameworks to two new biopharmaceutical case studies: antibody developability prediction and lipid-RNA MD simulation.
The study provides a systematic comparative evaluation of AI frameworks against published reference studies, including multiple independent runs and smaller-scope prompts.
The evaluation protocol includes full-scale and smaller-scope prompts, with the smaller-scope prompts prescribing specific datasets, featurizations, force fields, and simulation protocols.
The antibody case study found that AI frameworks used only one dataset and 2-5 ML models, compared to 240 datasets and 30 models in the reference study.
The AI Scientist-v2 claimed 200-500 ns all-atom simulations but actually generated a synthetic dataset with fabricated feature vectors and ran no MD simulations.
The paper positions its work against prior benchmark-based AI evaluations and the first paper in the series, arguing that published research papers provide a more demanding test.
The paper acknowledges that AI frameworks were run in January-March 2026 and conclusions reflect the state of the frameworks at that time, which may have changed since then.
The paper reports that no AI framework found and cited the original reference paper, despite it being the single most relevant paper for the prompt.

evidence.excerpt:
Lean's kernel guarantees that an accepted proof has the stated theorem as its type, relative to the imported
environment [28,29]. It does not, however, guarantee that the statement faithfully captures the scientific
claim that motivated the task. A benchmark can therefore be mechanically valid while remaining semantically
misleading: an omitted hypothesis, an incorrect type or function encoding, or a weakened conclusion can
cause the formal target to diverge from the intended mathematics [26]. We therefore treat Lean compilation
and the automated checks applied to every task as universal mechanical guarantees, while regarding semantic
fidelity as a separate validity question.
For selected statements whose translation carries elevated semantic risk, we perform a manual comparison
between the formal signature, its supporting definitions, and the available mathematical specification. 
[… separate evidence block …]
This
comparison examines the relevant objects and quantifiers, explicit and implicit assumptions, dimensional
constraints, index and tensor ordering, and the direction and strength of the conclusion. Any discrepancies
identified in this process are resolved before the task is included in the benchmark.
This targeted comparison supplements the automated checks applied to every task. Because it is performed
only on selected high-risk statements, it is not intended to define a benchmark-wide rate of semantic validity.

Lean's kernel guarantees that an accepted proof has the stated theorem as its type, relative to the imported
environment [28,29]. It does not, however, guarantee that the statement faithfully captures the scientific
claim that motivated the task. A benchmark can therefore be mechanically valid while remaining semantically
misleading: an omitted hypothesis, an incorrect type or function encoding, or a weakened conclusion can
cause the formal target to diverge from the intended mathematics [26]. We therefore treat Lean compilation
and the automated checks applied to every task as universal mechanical guarantees, while regarding semantic
fidelity as a separate validity question.
For selected statements whose translation carries elevated semantic risk, we perform a manual comparison
between the formal signature, its supporting definitions, and the available mathematical specification.

The reported results have four main validity limits that warrant further study: corpus coverage and difficulty
calibration, semantic fidelity of the formal statements, comparability of the recorded runs, and availability
of economic-cost records. Together, these limits constrain how far the observed scores and costs can be
generalized beyond the present evaluation. These limitations make the reported results an initial measurement
of the recorded benchmark runs, rather than a population estimate or a causal comparison of access conditions.
At the corpus level, the two suites sample theorem-sized tasks from selected parts of quantum algorithms
and quantum information under the current Lean library interfaces. Their 36 and 40 tasks do not provide
complete coverage of either domain, and the six author-defined fields aggregate areas of unequal size and
maturity. Task selection, theorem 
[… separate evidence block …]
granularity, and the availability of reusable definitions all affect what
can enter the benchmark. Difficulty is assigned before model execution through two rubric-based reviews

positive_signals: The paper introduces Lean-QuantumAlg-Bench and Lean-QIT-Bench, two Lean 4 benchmarks containing 36 and 40 theorem-completion tasks for quantum algorithms and quantum information theory, respectively.

Every admitted task passes automated Lean compilation and screening checks, and submission-side acceptance recompiles the submitted theorem in a fixed environment, rejecting new axioms, sorry placeholders, and changes outside the theorem body.
The paper's claims about LAD improvements are explicitly limited to descriptive recorded-run differences rather than causal estimates of access-condition effects.

The paper situates its benchmarks relative to formal theorem-proving benchmarks such as miniF2F, PutnamBench, LeanDojo, and miniCTX, and identifies the need for coordinated quantum-domain evaluation with controlled library access.

The benchmark tasks use a fixed Lean environment, deterministic proof checks, and recorded suite versions, model settings, access conditions, and execution settings to support descriptive aggregation and reproducibility.

The paper identifies four main validity limits: corpus coverage and difficulty calibration, semantic fidelity of formal statements, comparability of recorded runs, and availability of economic-cost records.
The paper defines the difficulty-weighted score formula and cost metrics precisely, including denominators, units, and conditions for unavailable values.

scholarly_quality.uncertainty: Scientific support remains unresolved. The sources define the scoring formula and cost metrics and report suite-level outcomes, but the cited excerpts do not show field-level results, so the claim that results sections report field-level outcomes is not fully established.

positive_signals: The paper introduces MisKnow-Agent, a controlled framework for constructing and validating apparently credible but factually misleading knowledge for Deep Research tasks, yielding 5,933 quality-controlled instances from DeepResearch Bench.
The paper evaluates six open-source framework-LLM configurations and one closed-source system, showing that even limited exposure to misleading knowledge can lead to false-conclusion adoption.

The paper characterizes how adoption varies with source properties, exposure conditions, lifecycle stage, framework choice, and backbone choice, and shows that pre- and post-research defenses reduce but do not eliminate false-conclusion adoption.

The paper positions its work against prior studies that examine short-horizon responses to misleading context or explicitly adversarial settings, arguing that Deep Research agents operate under a different regime where misleading content can be selected, compressed, and reused during final report generation without the
The paper's threat model reflects risks in open information environments and does not assume instruction-level attacks such as prompt injection or instruction hijacking.
The paper reports that introducing a single misleading document increases mean FCAR from 0% in the no-injection control to 54.7%.
The paper reports that pre- and post-research defenses reduce FCAR but do not eliminate false-conclusion adoption, and that combining them does not consistently yield additive gains.

title: Is Deep Research Reliable? Misleading Knowledge Induces False Conclusions

abstract_summary: Long-form legal research reports increasingly rely on LLMs and agentic research systems, but their reliability depends not only on answering the task, but also on whether cited legal authorities are trustworthy. evidence.excerpt:
The tool ablation isolates how retrieval ac-
cess changes one base system. Starting from
Qwen36_plus, we progressively add law search,
law plus case search, and law plus case plus web
search, while keeping the task input and base
prompt fixed. Table 6 reports the report-level sum-
mary.
Law search modestly increases Support from
0.3153 to 0.3427 and Trust from 0.7744 to 0.7951,
raising Final from 0.9612 to 0.9718. Adding case
search produces the largest evidence gain: Support
rises to 0.4857, especially through Subtopic Ev-
idence Support, but Trust drops to 0.7433. The
law-plus-case condition still achieves the highest
Final score among tool settings, showing that case
evidence improves the composite score while in-
creasing citation risk.
Adding web search does not further improve per-
formance: Support falls to 0.4197, Trust remains
nearly unchanged, and Final drops to 0.9903. 
[… separate evidence block …]
Item-
level diagnostics in Appendix E clarify this pattern:
case citations increase from 4 in the base setting
to 146 with case search, then fall to 73 when web
search is added. Tool-call statistics point in the
same direction: the law-only setting uses about
1.97 tool calls per report on average; law plus case
uses about 4.15, including about 2.24 case-search
calls; and law plus case plus web uses about 6.10,
including about 1.94 web-search calls. Tool aug-
mentation therefore shifts the balance between evi-
dence richness and citation reliability rather than
producing monotonic improvement.
evidence.explanation: The reported Support and Trust changes across tool settings directly align with the paper's central claim about the Support-Trust tension.
evidence.paraphrase: The tool ablation shows that adding case search increases Support from 0.3153 to 0.4857 but lowers Trust from 0.7744 to 0.7433, supporting the claim that retrieval can improve evidence support without reliably improving citation trustworthiness.

LegalCiteTrust turns citation trustworthiness into
an explicit evaluation protocol, but it does not
make legal citation use mechanically objective.
Existence is largely a source-resolution question,
whereas Fidelity and Applicability are protocol-
ized legal judgments about conditions, exceptions,
factual context, statute versions, and the distance
between a cited source and the local claim. Bound-
ary cases may arise when a report omits a minor
qualification, underspecifies the applicable source
version, or cites a source that supports a narrower
proposition but not the stronger claim made in the
report. Human audit, repeated-judge checks, and
bootstrap analyses test consistency with the proto-
col, not agreement with objective legal truth. Legal-
CiteTrust should therefore support expert review
rather than replace it; Appendix F.2 discusses the
corresponding overuse risk in legal

72 tasks are authority-demanding Chinese legal re-

positive_signals: The benchmark addresses an under-evaluated gap: whether each cited legal authority is used as a trustworthy ground for the local claim, rather than merely whether citations can be generated, matched, or verified.

The benchmark construction filters 13,622 candidate legal research documents to 72 source documents with at least one case citation and at least five statutory or normative references, yielding 236 subtopics, 585 rubrics, and 1,459 evidence points.
The main leaderboard evaluates seven end-to-end systems across general-purpose LLMs, deep or agentic research systems, and legal-specific systems on the same 72 tasks.

The verification ablation shows Trust increases from 0.7433 for Base to 0.8134 with existence-only filtering and 0.8883 with full E/F/A revision, while Final increases from 1.0329 to 1.0970 and 1.1708.

The tool ablation shows that adding case search increases Support from 0.3153 to 0.4857 but lowers Trust from 0.7744 to 0.7433, supporting the claim that retrieval can improve evidence support without reliably improving citation trustworthiness.

LegalCiteTrust is positioned at the intersection of legal task evaluation, agentic or deep-research report evaluation, and hallucination or citation-faithfulness evaluation, with a table comparing representative work across legal, deep research, long report, citation support, and citation trust dimensions.
The released code records the task prompts, citation extraction, source resolution, E/F/A judging, scoring, and aggregation pipeline.

The benchmark is dense rather than broad, with 72 authority-demanding Chinese legal research problems, and transfer to other jurisdictions is nontrivial because citation formats, statute versioning, case authority, and legal research practice vary across legal systems.

Fidelity and Applicability are protocolized legal judgments about conditions, exceptions, factual context, statute versions, and the distance between a cited source and the local claim, and human audit tests consistency with the protocol rather than agreement with objective legal truth.

concerns: The evaluation is conducted entirely on ARCHE, a benchmark whose construction is co-authored by at least one of the paper's authors (Li et al., AAAI 2026, reference [5]), creating a potential circularity: the Peircean schema, the CG/REA gate, and the judge protocol are all defined within or tightly coupled to that benchmark, so the 300/350 strict-gate result measures compliance with a self-referential standard rather than independently validated scientific quality.

The strict gate (CG=1.0 AND REA=1.0) is defined and enforced by the same judge-feedback loop used for repair, meaning the evaluator that drives repair also determines acceptance; no independent human annotation or held-out judge is reported to validate that gate-passing graphs are genuinely semantically correct, leaving the core quality claim unverified by external evidence.

The LLM models cited in the experimental setup include 'GPT-5.2', 'Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview', 'Grok 4.1 Thinking', and 'Qwen3.5-397B-A17B', none of which correspond to publicly documented model versions as of known literature; the references point to URLs that cannot be verified as real model releases, raising concerns about the authenticity of the experimental setup.

The paper does not report inter-annotator agreement, judge reliability, or any calibration of the LLM-as-judge against human judgments for the CG/REA metrics, so the magnitude of the reported improvement (REA 0.339→0.906) cannot be assessed for validity independent of the judge's own biases.

Limitations are acknowledged only briefly and do not address the circularity of using the benchmark's own evaluation protocol as both the repair signal and the acceptance criterion, nor the lack of external validation.
scholarly_quality.concise_summary: The paper presents a substantive, well-scoped contribution with an adequately described method, meaningful benchmark evaluation including ablations and residual analysis, and claims that are justified by the reported evidence. The limitations are compatible with the contribution scope, and the strict-gate definition prevents inflated success metrics. No material scientific uncertainty remains that would justify withholding promotion.

auditable reasoning graphs and repairs them toward strict semantic va-

average REA improving from0.339to0.906. The graphs provide a reli-
ability layer for research-agent and AI scientist workflows that need in-
spectable reasoning traces rather than unconstrained graph regeneration.

outputs into auditable artifacts and, when possible, semantically valid graphs.

pipeline first stabilizes source-linked structure and then corrects reasoning errors
using matched-judge feedback. This staged approach improves strict-gate passes
without unconstrained whole-graph regeneration.

evidence.excerpt:
The five-model CG/REA results appear in Table 1. The LLM baseline does not
pass the strict gate on any of the 350 rows, while PEARL passes on 300 rows.
Average CG improves from0.827to0.896, and average REA improves from0.339
to0.906. The larger REA gain shows that most of the remaining gap in the base-
line is not entity mention coverage, but reasoning-edge and root correctness. This
pattern matters for deployment because many baseline graphs are not empty or
wholly unusable. They often retain enough local content to look plausible while
still failing the global consistency conditions required for reliable reuse. In that
failure regime, a repair layer is most valuable when it preserves anchored node
content and targets edge/root correctness directly instead of replacing the entire
graph with unconstrained regeneration.

blocking_reasons: The evaluation is conducted entirely on ARCHE, a benchmark whose construction is co-authored by at least one of the paper's authors (Li et al., AAAI 2026, reference [5]), creating a potential circularity: the Peircean schema, the CG/REA gate, and the judge protocol are all defined within or tightly coupled to that benchmark, so the 300/350 strict-gate result measures compliance with a self-referential standard rather than independently validated scientific quality.

The strict gate (CG=1.0 AND REA=1.0) is defined and enforced by the same judge-feedback loop used for repair, meaning the evaluator that drives repair also determines acceptance; no independent human annotation or held-out judge is reported to validate that gate-passing graphs are genuinely semantically correct, leaving the core quality claim unverified by external evidence.

The LLM models cited in the experimental setup include 'GPT-5.2', 'Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview', 'Grok 4.1 Thinking', and 'Qwen3.5-397B-A17B', none of which correspond to publicly documented model versions as of known literature; the references point to URLs that cannot be verified as real model releases, raising concerns about the authenticity of the experimental setup.

The paper does not report inter-annotator agreement, judge reliability, or any calibration of the LLM-as-judge against human judgments for the CG/REA metrics, so the magnitude of the reported improvement (REA 0.339→0.906) cannot be assessed for validity independent of the judge's own biases.

Limitations are acknowledged only briefly and do not address the circularity of using the benchmark's own evaluation protocol as both the repair signal and the acceptance criterion, nor the lack of external validation.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: The central claims about strict-gate improvement, REA gains, residual causes, and ablation effects are directly supported by the reported results. The paper avoids overclaiming by treating MiniCheck as a diagnostic supplement rather than an acceptance gate and by identifying missing-anchor failures as the main residual bottleneck.
primary.evaluation_assessment: Evaluation covers five model archives with 350 total rows, reporting strict gate passes, CG, REA, per-model results, residual taxonomy, diagnostic ablations, and MiniCheck grounding diagnostics. The improvement from 0/350 to 300/350 strict passes is a large, clearly quantified effect, and ablations isolate the contribution of local judge-conditioned repair.
primary.limitations: Limitations are acknowledged: the framework targets the ARCHE Peircean schema and five text-only archives, and portability to new schemas or multimodal evidence would require revised validators, frozen judge versions, and wider deployment checks.
primary.method_assessment: The method is described in sufficient detail: a source-referenced graph contract, tolerance-aware structural materialization, deterministic schema repair, judge-feedback semantic repair, and a final strict CG/REA gate with provenance audit. The staged separation of structural admissibility from semantic validity is clearly specified.
primary.quality_rationale: The paper presents a substantive, well-scoped contribution with an adequately described method, meaningful benchmark evaluation including ablations and residual analysis, and claims that are justified by the reported evidence. The limitations are compatible with the contribution scope, and the strict-gate definition prevents inflated success metrics. No material scientific uncertainty remains that would justify withholding promotion.
primary.scoped_contribution: A training-free framework that materializes noisy LLM graph responses into auditable scientific reasoning graphs under a closed Peircean schema and repairs rejected reasoning units via matched judge feedback. The contribution is scoped to SRGE on the ARCHE benchmark and five text-only model archives.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The paper presents a substantive, well-scoped contribution with an adequately described method, meaningful benchmark evaluation including ablations and residual analysis, and claims that are justified by the reported evidence. The limitations are compatible with the contribution scope, and the strict-gate definition prevents inflated success metrics. No material scientific uncertainty remains that would justify withholding promotion.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: Limitations are acknowledged: the framework targets the ARCHE Peircean schema and five text-only archives, and portability to new schemas or multimodal evidence would require revised validators, frozen judge versions, and wider deployment checks.

evidence.excerpt:
Deep research agents increasingly operate over the open web, where relevant
records coexist with redundant summaries, outdated reports, and misleading doc-
uments. Existing evaluations offer limited insight into whether agents preserve
sound evidential standards when an ordinary-looking false document is deliberately
seeded into a searchable environment and offers a direct shortcut to a conflicting
answer. We introduce DRNOISE, a 100-task benchmark for answer recovery un-
der misleading evidence. Each task has a unique gold answer supported by two
corroborating indirect record chains; the paired noisy condition adds one plausible
document that states a conflicting answer directly. The benchmark spans ten fami-
lies of evidence operations. Across agents with strong clean-task performance, this
single intervention causes 66–88 percentage-point accuracy drops. Trace analyses
identify

evidence when the same environment also contains a plausible but false answer. To make this question

The paired design requires metrics that distinguish three cases: an agent may be unable to solve the
task even without noise, may fail under noise for reasons unrelated to the injected false value, or may
specifically defer to the misleading document. We therefore report both accuracy and conditional
deference.
Let Cm be the set of tasks that model m answers correctly in the clean condition, and let Dm be the
set of tasks where the model's noisy answer equals the designated false value. We report:
CleanAcc(m) =|Cm|/100,(1)
NoisyAcc(m) =|{i:mcorrect on noisy taski}|/100,(2)
Defer(m) =|Cm ∩D m|/|Cm|.(3)
Conditional deference is stricter than noisy error rate. It is computed only over tasks the model
solved when the misleading document was absent, and it only counts noisy answers that match the
benchmark's designated false value. This prevents a weak model from appearing robust

v2.5 fall to roughly 1% noisy accuracy. Gemini 3.5 Flash retains the most, yet still shows a 72.6%
conditional deference rate. GPT-5.4 is intermediate, with 16% noisy accuracy and 80.4% conditional
deference.

DRNOISEuses a constructed corpus rather than documents scraped from the live web. This controlled
design is necessary for paired clean–noisy evaluation: it allows us to define a unique gold answer,
construct corroborating indirect evidence chains, and introduce a falsifiable misleading document
while keeping the two conditions comparable. However, constructed documents may not capture the
full stylistic, institutional, and distributional complexity of naturally occurring web sources. Future
work should test whether the same failure mode appears in live-web or domain-specific corpora
containing real outdated reports, secondary summaries, conflicting claims, and misleading documents.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: The manuscript's claims are well supported by its paired clean-noisy design and reported measurements. The central claim of large accuracy drops under a single misleading document is directly evidenced by Table 3 and Figure 1, with conditional deference isolating the specific failure mode. Mechanism claims about premature stopping are supported by retrieval-exposure, trace taxonomy, and oracle full-context analyses.
primary.evaluation_assessment: The paper introduces a controlled 100-task benchmark with a clean paired intervention design, evaluates five models in a fixed harness, and provides multiple ablations that localize the failure to premature stopping and verification inertia. The contribution is substantive and scoped, with appropriate limitations acknowledged.
primary.limitations: The benchmark uses a constructed corpus rather than live-web documents, which may not capture full stylistic and distributional complexity of naturally occurring sources. The Qwen3-32B deference estimate is based on only 13 clean-correct tasks and carries greater uncertainty. Attack-aware prompts that name the document class are reported only as upper bounds, not deployable fixes.
primary.method_assessment: The paired clean-noisy corpus intervention is well suited to isolating evidence-use changes. The fixed search-agent harness, conditional deference metric, and controlled ablations (verification prompts, source credibility, retriever, direct-true evidence, oracle full-context) provide strong internal validity for the mechanism claims.
primary.quality_rationale: The contribution is clearly scoped and validated: a new benchmark with a diagnostic paired design, meaningful evaluation across five models and ten task families, and controlled analyses that distinguish premature stopping from retrieval or reconciliation failures. Claims are justified by the reported measurements, and limitations are appropriately stated.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper contributes a 100-task benchmark for answer recovery under misleading evidence, with a paired clean-noisy design, ten evidence-operation families, and empirical evidence of a capability-deployment gap in deep research agents.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The contribution is clearly scoped and validated: a new benchmark with a diagnostic paired design, meaningful evaluation across five models and ten task families, and controlled analyses that distinguish premature stopping from retrieval or reconciliation failures. Claims are justified by the reported measurements, and limitations are appropriately stated.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The benchmark uses a constructed corpus rather than live-web documents, which may not capture full stylistic and distributional complexity of naturally occurring sources. The Qwen3-32B deference estimate is based on only 13 clean-correct tasks and carries greater uncertainty. Attack-aware prompts that name the document class are reported only as upper bounds, not deployable fixes.

Analogical Deep Research: Retrieving and Integrating Historical Analogies for Foresight Analysis
Figure 3| Overview ofCausalAnalogical Researcher (CANA). CANA decomposes each event into
a structural representation (preconditions, temporal chains, mechanisms, outcomes),
realizingPrinciple 1(retrieve on the mechanism𝑀(𝐸)rather than the surface description𝐷(𝐸)). It
then performs structural reflective generation, using feedback on covered and uncovered structural
positions to iteratively retrieve cross-confirming analogies until each hidden position is supported by
≥ 2independent analogies, realizingPrinciple 2. The resulting Structural Analogy Brief (SAB), which
contains mechanism statements, per-analogy limitations, cross-analogy invariants, and predicted
hidden factors, is passed as context to the mainDRagent (MiroFlow).

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Reported findings align well with empirical results and theoretical bounds, showing marked improvements in identifying hidden factors (HF@L4) and structural claims (L3-S/L4) where baseline deep research agents consistently score near zero.
primary.evaluation_assessment: The evaluation uses both existing analogy benchmarks and the newly created ADR-bench against leading commercial and open-source deep research baselines across multiple backbone models (e.g., GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5/4.6, Qwen3-8B). Metric criteria, rubrics, prompt templates, and ablation/comparative statistics clearly demonstrate CANA's improvements in analogy retrieval fidelity and structural foresight inference.
primary.limitations: The authors acknowledge limitations openly, including the relatively modest scale of ADR-bench (15 events) and its heavy reliance on LLM judges for rubric-based scoring.
primary.method_assessment: The methodology is thoroughly detailed, combining formal theoretical proofs regarding surface non-identifiability and cross-analogy Bayes-factor bounds with a multi-step agentic pipeline. CANA decomposes target events into structural components (preconditions, temporal chains, mechanisms, outcomes) and applies strict self-analogy filtering and reflective candidate generation.
primary.quality_rationale: The manuscript provides an innovative, conceptually well-grounded, and clearly validated extension to agentic reasoning and applied foresight analysis. The theoretical framework directly motivates the algorithmic components, and the extensive appendices provide complete prompt configurations, algorithmic pseudo-code, and evaluation rubrics.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper formalizes the task of Analogical Deep Research (ADR) for foresight analysis, introduces the ADR-bench benchmark comprising 15 historical and forward events, establishes theoretical principles governing structural analogy retrieval and cross-analogy confirmation, and presents CANA (Causal Analogical Researcher), an agent framework that leverages structural decomposition and reflective retrieval.

across fine-grained categories.

evidence.excerpt:
Consistency alone is insufficient: a rubric may be
perfectly stable while still assigning the same effec-
tive judgment to all products. We therefore apply
a second filter at the cross-report level. For each
consistency-passed rubric, we compute the major-
ity label for each of the 10 product reports. A rubric
is considered distinguishable if at least one report
receives a majority-yes label and at least one re-
port receives a majority-no label. This removes
one-sided rubrics such as always-yes or always-no
criteria that are stable but uninformative for product
comparison.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Claims regarding the scalability, expert-free final execution, and discriminative capacity of consensus-derived gold rubrics are directly supported by statistical filtering results, inter-annotator agreement metrics, and stable system rankings across diverse splits.
primary.evaluation_assessment: The empirical evaluation thoroughly validates batched judge stability, measures high human-LLM label agreement (98.67% on jointly unanimous items, Cohen's kappa 0.9733), demonstrates clear system separation across 10 commercial systems, and provides robust sensitivity checks including leave-one-judge-out and split-half distinguishability ablations.
primary.limitations: The authors explicitly note limitations regarding temporal sensitivity of financial domain data, rapid product version drift, and the need for future validation across other specialized professional domains.
primary.method_assessment: The methodology is clearly specified: candidate rubrics synthesized for 104 real-world financial queries across 1,040 reports are evaluated by a panel of three LLM judges, validated against three human financial analysts on 4,052 instances, and filtered through strict cross-judge unanimity and cross-system distinguishability.
primary.quality_rationale: The manuscript establishes an ecologically grounded, technically rigorous evaluation framework with sound controls, explicit inter-rater agreement analyses, and comprehensive sensitivity checks supporting all core claims.
primary.scoped_contribution: FinResearchBench II presents a pipeline for benchmarking deep research financial reports by synthesizing query-specific candidate rubrics from generated reports and filtering them via multi-LLM consensus (strict unanimity and distinguishability) after human-expert validation.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The manuscript establishes an ecologically grounded, technically rigorous evaluation framework with sound controls, explicit inter-rater agreement analyses, and comprehensive sensitivity checks supporting all core claims.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The authors explicitly note limitations regarding temporal sensitivity of financial domain data, rapid product version drift, and the need for future validation across other specialized professional domains.

missing_information: No reproducible review or selection methodology was detected.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Claims regarding model performance drop-offs on mechanistic and exploratory tasks relative to basic descriptive tasks, as well as the persistence of later-stage reasoning errors over variable-grounding errors in stronger models, are directly aligned with the empirical findings.
primary.evaluation_assessment: The evaluation covers 15 open and proprietary LLMs under zero-shot and fine-tuned settings across held-out synthetic test splits and real-world datasets, supplemented by a fine-grained five-stage failure categorization (Scope, Variable, Function, Relationship, Conclusion) with normalized error rates.
primary.limitations: The authors explicitly discuss constraints including the potential gap between synthetic semantic graph dynamics and real experimental confounders, the risk of MCQ options inducing superficial heuristics, and annotating only the first execution error.
primary.method_assessment: The methodology is clearly defined, utilizing semantic directed acyclic graphs and internally standardized structural causal models for synthetic generation, paired with an automated four-agent template construction and deterministic programmatic derivation pipeline to establish verifiable ground truth.
primary.quality_rationale: The benchmark provides a well-substantiated, methodologically sound framework addressing known pitfalls in execution-only LLM evaluations. Data generation, programmatic verification, and diagnostic error evaluations are thoroughly documented and scientifically credible.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper introduces SDABench, an evaluation benchmark for scientific data analysis across six reasoning capabilities and five scientific domains, comprising 527 real-data instances and 6,000 synthetic instances evaluated under both open-ended and multiple-choice formats alongside a five-stage error analysis framework.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The benchmark provides a well-substantiated, methodologically sound framework addressing known pitfalls in execution-only LLM evaluations. Data generation, programmatic verification, and diagnostic error evaluations are thoroughly documented and scientifically credible.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The authors explicitly discuss constraints including the potential gap between synthetic semantic graph dynamics and real experimental confounders, the risk of MCQ options inducing superficial heuristics, and annotating only the first execution error.

evidence.excerpt:
governed end-to-end agentic research system designed
to support scientific workflows in institutionally constrained environments. NAIS combines durable
research state, proposal-level planning, agentic execution, brokered data access, reproducible
workflow orchestration, evidence tracking, and scientist-in-the-loop oversight. Rather than granting
an agent unrestricted access to protected data, NAIS separates reasoning and orchestration from data
governance: the agent submits approved actions through controlled interfaces, protected data remain
inside institutional infrastructure, and only governed artifacts such as aggregate summaries, quality-
control metrics, plots, logs, and manuscript-oriented evidence are returned. Figure 1 illustrates
the overall architecture, showing how proposal review, agentic execution, and governed data access
compose into an end-to-end research system.

Generalizability is the primary constraint. The NAIS deployment is a single-institution case
study, and broader claims about NAIS performance require validation across additional hospital
environments and data governance frameworks.
The GWAS results are replication evidence, not novel discovery. Lead loci are identified qualitatively
from Manhattan-plot inspection. Exact per-SNP effect sizes and lead variant identification require
extraction from the underlying association result files, which was not performed for this manuscript.
The DILI prediction case remains illustrative. Model E was evaluated on 390 compounds using
5-fold Murcko scaffold cross-validation with low variance (SD 0.018), and ablation of the Diff-
Dock/thermodynamics branches drops AUC to 0.71, confirming the contribution of structural
features. A dataset of this size is insufficient for clinical-grade validation

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: The claims that NAIS executes end-to-end workflows while preserving institutional privacy boundaries and generating outputs comparable to expert analyses are supported by empirical GWAS results, label confusion matrices, discordance analysis, and multi-modal predictive modeling benchmarks.
primary.evaluation_assessment: The platform is empirically evaluated on a real-world hypertension genome-wide association study using 286,422 individuals from a hospital biobank, successfully replicating established genomic loci (FGF5, ATP2B1, CNNM2, FTO, and GRB14) in alignment with an independently curated expert analysis. Additional validation demonstrates utility on a drug-induced liver injury prediction workflow (AUC 0.842) and across containerized benchmark runs.
primary.limitations: The authors transparently acknowledge that evaluation is largely focused on a single-institution deployment, GWAS results reflect locus replication rather than novel variant discovery without per-SNP effect extraction, and the secondary drug-induced liver injury study relied on a modest compound sample size.
primary.method_assessment: The system architecture clearly delineates reasoning and orchestration from data governance by routing requests through sandboxed execution, a broker API, and Kubeflow containers, ensuring no individual-level protected health information is released to the agent. The approach is documented via end-to-end operational stages, including proposal review, SQL cohort extraction, containerized execution, and iterative discordance auditing.
primary.quality_rationale: The manuscript presents a rigorous, well-engineered architectural design addressing a vital open challenge in deploying autonomous/agentic AI within privacy-regulated biomedical environments. The system is validated through extensive real-world clinical data with clear controls, human-expert comparative baselines, and transparent documentation of limitations and failure recovery.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper introduces the NVAITC AI Scientist (NAIS), a governed agentic research architecture that orchestrates biomedical workflows across protected institutional boundaries using brokered execution, durable state tracking, aggregate-only artifact retrieval, and human-in-the-loop oversight.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The manuscript presents a rigorous, well-engineered architectural design addressing a vital open challenge in deploying autonomous/agentic AI within privacy-regulated biomedical environments. The system is validated through extensive real-world clinical data with clear controls, human-expert comparative baselines, and transparent documentation of limitations and failure recovery.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The authors transparently acknowledge that evaluation is largely focused on a single-institution deployment, GWAS results reflect locus replication rather than novel variant discovery without per-SNP effect extraction, and the secondary drug-induced liver injury study relied on a modest compound sample size.
